                24 SEP 2026 10:16PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The third day carried the 9th India International Water Week 2026 deeper into its technical programme, into the forward-looking questions of climate risk, early warning, glacial lake monitoring, water pricing and the financing of resilient water infrastructure. Sessions ran in parallel across the Water Leaders' Forum, Country Forum, Practitioners' Forum, Thematic Forum and Start-Up Forum. The Thematic Forum closed the third of its seven sub-themes and moved through the fourth and fifth.
The day also widened the Week's international reach. The Start-Up Forum gave startups, MSMEs and academia a platform to pitch problem-driven water solutions. On the sidelines, a bilateral meeting advanced India-Netherlands cooperation, with two tripartite MoUs signed.
India-Netherlands Bilateral Meeting
On the sidelines of the 9th India International Water Week-2026, a bilateral meeting between the Shri C R Patil, Minister of Jal Shakti and H.E. Mr. Jaap Slootmaker, Vice Minister for Infrastructure and Water Management, Netherlands, was held at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi. Shri Raj Bhushan Choudhary, Minister of State, Ministry of Jal Shakti, Shri Ishwarsinh Patel, Minister of State for Water Resources and Water Supply (Independent Charge), joined the meeting, along with H. E Marissa Gerard, Ambassador of the Kingdom of the Netherlands to India.
During the event, a tripartite MoU was signed between Central Water Commission, Kalpasar, Deptt. Govt. of Gujarat and Deltares, Netherlands for technical support. Another tripartite MoU was signed between CWC, Kalpasar Deptt. of Govt. of Gujarat and TU Delft Netherlands for capacity building and trainings. The MoUs will facilitate technical collaboration through sharing of Dutch expertise and advanced engineering practices for the planning, design and implementation of the project.
Country Forum (CF)
CF-4 on Private Capital Mobilisation in the Water Sector, convened with the World Bank, was chaired by Shri Baldeo Purushartha, Joint Secretary, DEA, GOI and co-chaired by Smt. Roshika Singh, Principal Country Officer, IFC India. The session opened with a keynote by Shri Saroj Kumar Jha, Global Water Director, World Bank, and was moderated by Mr. William Rex, Practice Manager for Water, World Bank, with Jain Irrigations, IFC India, Coca-Cola,VA Tech Wabag, Tata Capital, the Maharashtra Institution for Transformation (MITRA) and the Uttar Pradesh State Transformation Commission, on the reforms and financing mechanisms needed to unlock private investment in urban water, wastewater and irrigation.
Water Leaders’ Forum (WLF)
WLF-3 on Improving Water Use Efficiency Using State-of-the-Art Technology in the Water Resources Sector, convened with the CII Water Institute, was chaired by P. C. Vyas, Principal Secretary, (Water Resources) Government of Gujarat, and co-chaired by Smt. Shilpa Nischal, Executive Director, CII Water Institute, with Grundfos, Murugappa Water Technology, Ion Exchange, Kritsnam Technologies and NITI Aayog, on smart metering, monitoring and technology for water-use efficiency.
WLF-4 on Climate Risk Assessment for Water Security, convened with the National Institute of Hydrology, Roorkee, was chaired by Prof. Nagesh Kumar, Professor, IISc Bangalore, and co-chaired by Dr. Y. R. S. Rao, Director, NIH Roorkee, with ICHARM (Japan), IIT Bombay, IISc Bangalore, CWC and IIT Delhi, on integrating climate risk assessment into water governance and planning frameworks.
WLF-5 on Embedding Climate Action in Water Governance and Policies, convened with CEEW, was chaired by Shri Jogindra Singh IAS, Project Director, State Mission for Clean Ganga, Govt. of Uttar Pradesh, and co-chaired by Ms. Noa Amsalem, Water Attache, Embassy of Israel, with IIT Guwahati, WELL Labs Bengaluru, the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, Google, Council on Energy, Environment and Water and DCM Shriram, on shifting from managing climate risk to building resilience through governance reform.
WLF-6 on Climate-Resilient Adaptation Measures in Water Resources, convened with the National Dam Safety Authority was chaired by Shri Rakesh Kashyap, Chairman, National Dam Safety Authority and co-chaired by Shri Manoj Kumar Acharya, Former Chief Engineer, BODHI, Madhya Pradesh Water Resources Department, with IIT Delhi, HCL Foundation, IMD, GIZ and NDMA, addressed hydrological modelling for dams under a changing climate, glacial lake outburst floods, and the structural rehabilitation of earthen and rockfill dams, drawing on international financing experience for climate-resilient dam infrastructure.
Practitioners’ Forum (PF)
PF-5 on Session on Best Practices, convened with the National Water Mission, was chaired by Shri Rajesh Toppo, Secretary, Water Resources, Government of Chhattisgarh, and co-chaired by Shri Atul Jain, Former Chairman, Central Water Commission, with district collectors and municipal commissioners from Tripura, Telangana and Surat; and Himalayan Environmental Studies and Conservation Organization, Ministry of Rural Development and The Rainwater Project, on integrating global best practices with the Ministry of Jal Shakti's efforts; the Jal Jeevan Mission now reports about 81.5% of rural households with tap water connections.
PF-6 on Water Disputes and Resolution, was chaired by Dr. Srinivas Chokkakula, President and Chief Executive, Centre for Policy Research and co-chaired by Shri P. Dorje Gyamba, Chairman, Godavari River Management Board, with the CWC, Supreme Court advocates, the National Water Academy, Pune, and river-basin management board representatives, examined Alternative Dispute Resolution mechanisms and the proposed Disputes Resolution Committee under the Inter-State River Water Disputes framework.
PF-7 on Jal-Sanskriti and HARIT Pathways: India's Water Heritage for a Resilient Future, was chaired by Dr. Murli Manohar Joshi, Padma Vibhushan, Former Union Minister, Ministry of Human Resource Development, on connecting India's traditional water culture, its sacred rivers, temple tanks and stepwells, with modern, climate-resilient water management, and on carrying that heritage into community-led conservation.
Thematic Forum (TF)
Six Thematic Forum sessions ran through the day, presenting shortlisted papers, closing the third of the Forum's seven sub-themes and moving through the fourth and fifth.
Sub-theme 3 and Sub-theme 4, Water in Climate-Related Risk:
TF-9 Data-Driven Governance
, chaired by Shri Sher Singh, Chairman, Ganga Flood Control Commission and Member (Floods), CWC, and co-chaired by Shri S. G. Bhartariya, Member (SAM), Central Ground Water Board with the National Water Informatics Centre, BISAG-N and the Government of Andhra Pradesh;
TF-10 Early Warning System for Climate Risk Reduction
, chaired by Dr. Krishna Vatsa, Member, National Disaster Management Authority, and co-chaired by Dr. D.R. Pattanaik, Scientist-G, India Meteorological Department;
TF-11 Monitoring of Glacial Lake Outburst
, chaired by Shri D. P. Mathuria, Chief Engineer (P&DO), Central Water Commission, and co-chaired by Dr. Surjeet Singh, Scientist 'G' & Head Centre for Cryosphere & Climate Change Studies (C4S), NIH Roorkee; and
TF-12 Climate Change: Erratic Precipitation
, was chaired by Dr. D.S. Pai, Scientist-G, India Meteorological Department and co-chaired by Dr. Ankur Srivastava, Scientist E, Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology, Pune with the India Meteorological Department, CWPRS Pune, NIH Roorkee and CWC. Papers ranged over water informatics and AI-assisted data governance, drought and flood forecasting, AI-powered dam-safety early warning, glacial lake outburst flood vulnerability and monitoring across the Himalaya, and long-term rainfall and temperature trends under a changing climate. Among the papers were the indigenous HIM JHEEL NETRA glacial-lake monitoring system, a national-scale flood forecasting system, erosion modelling on the Brahmaputra, and geophysical investigations for dam safety.
Sub-theme 5, Innovative Financing Models:
TF-13 Public-Private Partnerships for Water Finance and Innovative Financing Models
, was chaired by Mr. Takeshi Ueda, Director, South Asia, Sector Department 2, Agriculture, Food, Nature, and Rural Development Sector Group, Asian Development Bank with co-chair Shri Rajesh Advani, Senior Water Specialist, World Bank, with the Asian Development Bank; and
TF-14 Policy for Water User Charges
, was chaired by Shri Sanjay Marwah, Member, Haryana Water Resources Authority, and co-chaired by Shri Subrata Singh, Executive Director, Foundation for Ecological Society. Papers examined green finance for WASH infrastructure, solar power potential along the Ken-Betwa link, and the restructuring of water user charges, including a comparative analysis of CGWA guidelines and AI-based canal-release optimisation, and made the case for water user charges as a lever for the long-term sustainability of irrigation.
Start-Up Forum (SUF)
)
The Start-Up Forum, chaired by Prof. Umesh V. Waghmare, Secretary, Department of Science and Technology and co-chaired by Col. Saurabh Sanyal, Secretary General, ASSOCHAM showcased problem-driven solutions from startups, MSMEs and academia across water resources management, wastewater treatment, irrigation efficiency and smart water systems, including prototypes developed through partnerships between startups, industry and academia. The forum also provided startups with an opportunity to present practical, deployable solutions to a panel of experts and investors.
The Ministry has also strengthened engagement with academic institutions and students to provide them with first-hand exposure to the challenges and opportunities in the water sector.
After having several meetings with the AICTE in coordination with Ministry of Education last year,
Jal Seva Adhyayan
initiative is being implemented in collaboration with AICTE. 49 teams, comprising students and faculty, visited 132 villages across the country from February till April 2026. They gained first-hand exposure to rural drinking water service delivery and submitted detailed field reports based on their observations. Around 50 participating students also joined the Roundtable Conference with African Ambassadors at Bharat Mandapam. Following the roundtable, a special interaction session titled
“Peyjal Ki Baat: Jal Shakti Minister ke Saath”
was organised, providing students a unique opportunity to engage directly with the leadership of the Ministry of Jal Shakti and discuss challenges, innovations and opportunities in the water sector.
The interaction highlighted the importance of youth participation, innovation and community engagement in strengthening the country's water sector. Students were encouraged to take their learnings beyond the classroom, apply their technical knowledge to real-world challenges and contribute towards building a Viksit Bharat 2047. The discussion focused on the transformative impact of the Jal Jeevan Mission on rural lives, the importance of safe drinking water, water quality surveillance through community participation, the growing role of digital technology and AI, and the need for innovative, practical and scalable solutions to address emerging water-sector challenges.
Addressing the students, Shri C R Patil, Union Minister of Jal Shakti, emphasised that the Jal Jeevan Mission is not merely an infrastructure programme but a transformational initiative linked to health, dignity, women's empowerment and quality of life. He urged students to develop innovative and cost-effective technological solutions for the water sector and stressed the importance of dialogue and consensus in resolving water-related challenges.
Shri Raj Bhushan Choudhary, Union Minister of State for Jal Shakti, encouraged students to study global best practices, leverage AI, digital technologies and social media, and identify solutions emerging from rural communities and grassroots innovators.
Shri Ashok K.K. Meena, Secretary, Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation, underlined the need to expose engineering students to ground-level realities of rural water supply systems and informed that, in collaboration with AICTE, efforts are underway to introduce water governance-related academic courses and expand the outreach of Jal Seva Adhyayan to engineering institutions nationwide.
Smt. Archana Varma, Secretary, Ministry of Water Resources, highlighted the transformative potential of information technology and artificial intelligence in water governance and called upon students to apply their technical expertise in public service, innovation and sustainable water management for national development.
Shri Kamal Kishore Soan, Additional Secretary and Mission Director, National Jal Jeevan Mission, welcomed the panelists and the students to the interactive session. He briefed about the
Jal Seva Adhyayan
, and the upcoming water management course by AICTE.
Technical Sessions
The first technical session, “Water Supply Systems: O&M, Infrastructure & Source Sustainability,” focused on strengthening the long-term sustainability of rural water supply systems. Four papers were presented covering themes including GIS-based assessment of water supply infrastructure, water pricing strategies, water footprint assessment for sustainable water resources management, and approaches to strengthening community ownership in piped drinking water systems. The discussions highlighted the importance of effective operation and maintenance, infrastructure and asset management, financial sustainability, and community participation in ensuring reliable water services.
The second technical session, “Water Quality, Safety & Emerging Contaminants,” focused on water safety and quality management in the context of emerging challenges. Five papers examined community-led climate-resilient interventions for water security, evaluation of field test kits for water safety planning, emerging contaminants and environmental laws, water quality challenges in India, and the use of digital tools for tracking water refill stations. The presentations highlighted the need for stronger water quality monitoring, water safety planning, community participation, and technology-enabled approaches.
Another session, “Financing, Economic Models & Techno-Economic Solutions,” deliberated on approaches to improving the financial and technological sustainability of water and sanitation services. Four papers covered innovative models for rural water supply, wastewater treatment and cost recovery, local economic models for sustaining rural drinking water services, and low-cost atmospheric water harvesting solutions. The session highlighted the role of appropriate technologies, local economic models, capacity building, and innovative approaches in supporting sustainable water services.
The fourth technical session, “Climate Resilience, Nature-Based Solutions & Sanitation/Other,” focused on approaches for strengthening the resilience of WASH systems in the face of climate-related challenges. Four papers covered digital intelligence and machine learning applications in sewage sludge management, sanitation innovation through start-ups and public-private partnerships, approaches to building water consciousness, and AI-enabled mechanised and robotic operation and maintenance of WASH infrastructure. The discussions highlighted the role of technology, innovation, partnerships and systems strengthening in addressing emerging challenges in water and sanitation.

title: Indo-Africa Roundtable on WASH Held as part of Second India International WASH Conference During 9th IIWW 2026
subtitle:
The Roundtable Brings Together Ambassadors of 22 African Countries, International Delegates and Scientists to Explore Opportunities For Collaboration In WASH

The Deliberation Focus on knowledge exchange, capacity building, digital innovation, community-led service delivery and climate-resilient WASH solutions
date:

content:
As part of the
Second India International WASH Conference
being organised during the
9th India International Water Week (IIWW) 2026
, the Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation (DDWS), Ministry of Jal Shakti, Government of India, today convened a high-level
Indo-Africa Roundtable on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH)
at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi to deliberate on shared water and sanitation challenges and explore opportunities for future cooperation.
The roundtable brought together Ambassadors and representatives of 22 African countries, senior officials of the Government of India, development partners, international organisations. AICTE-affiliated engineering students from the National Capital Region are called to witness the deliberations.
Setting the Context
Shri Ashok K. K. Meena, Secretary, DDWS
, highlighted that India's experience in rural water supply and sanitation extends beyond physical infrastructure and is fundamentally about public health, dignity, women's empowerment and community ownership. He emphasised that
strong political commitment and local institutional ownership have been central to India's progress
under the Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) and Swachh Bharat Mission-Gramin (SBM-G). Drawing attention to the
decentralised governance framework
adopted in India, he underlined the critical role played by Gram Panchayats and Village Water and Sanitation Committees in planning, operation, monitoring and sustainability of rural services.
Shri Meena further highlighted that over 2.48 million women have been trained in the use of Field Testing Kits for water-quality surveillance, making women active participants in local water governance. He also recalled the transformative impact of Swachh Bharat Mission-Gramin, which converted sanitation into a nationwide people's movement through behavioural change, local leadership and community participation. Emphasising the importance of sustainability, he outlined five key lessons from India's experience: strong political leadership, empowered local governments, investment in people alongside infrastructure, planning for operation and maintenance from the outset, and the use of simple and interoperable digital systems for accountability and service delivery.
Secretary DDWS, said that India is honored to share its operational knowledge, digital approaches and experience in community governance, while learning from innovations and experiences emerging across Africa. The objective of this deliberation is
to learn from one another and strengthen approaches that can deliver safe water, dignified sanitation and resilient services for communities
. Such cooperation can
contribute meaningfully to the achievement of Sustainable Development Goal 6.
Presenting India's experience in rural drinking-water service delivery,
Shri Kamal Kishore Soan, Additional Secretary and Mission Director, National Jal Jeevan Mission
, highlighted the unprecedented scale of investments made that shows political will. Launch of Jal Jeevan Mission on 15 August 2019 marked a decisive shift towards ensuring functional tap-water connections for every rural household. The experience has reinforced the importance of political commitment, public investment, coordinated implementation and community participation.  He noted that these lessons can contribute to the wider exchange of knowledge among countries seeking to strengthen reliable and sustainable rural water services. He presented that tap-water coverage has increased from 32.4 million rural households in 2019 to over 159.4 million households today and explained how the Mission has addressed long-standing challenges of limited piped-water supply, non-functional schemes, excessive dependence on groundwater and water-quality concerns through a combination of infrastructure development, source sustainability measures, water-quality monitoring and community participation.
He informed that India's rural water-management strategy is increasingly focused on
sustainability, including a gradual shift from groundwater dependence towards greater utilisation of surface-water sources
. He also showcased
Sujalam Bharat
, India's emerging Digital Public Infrastructure for rural water governance, which aims to provide
source-to-tap visibility
,
digital asset mapping, data-driven governance and improved service management through a common interoperable digital backbone
.
Presenting India's sanitation journey,
Ms. Aishvarya Singh, Joint Secretary and Mission Director, Swachh Bharat Mission-Gramin
, highlighted how the the Mission transformed sanitation into a peoples’ movement through unprecedented community participation and behavioural change. She noted that more than 120 million household toilets have been constructed since 2014, helping India achieve
universal sanitation coverage and attain SDG target 6.2 ahead of schedule.
She stated that SBM-G has now moved beyond toilet construction towards sustainable rural sanitation service delivery. The current focus includes solid and liquid waste management, visual cleanliness, ODF Plus Model Villages, digital monitoring systems and institutional mechanisms for regular assessment of sanitation services. She also highlighted recent initiatives such as Swachh Seva Aandolan and efforts to institutionalise sanitation service delivery through local governments, digital systems and community-led verification. Stressing the importance of behaviour change, she observed that sanitation outcomes can be sustained only when communities themselves become custodians of cleanliness and public-health gains.
Delivering the global perspective,
Mr. Saroj Kumar Jha, Global Director-Water, World Bank,
described India's water and sanitation transformation as one of the most significant examples of large-scale development change witnessed across developing countries. He observed that strong political leadership, institutional coordination, innovative financing, public investment and community participation were key factors behind the success.
Highlighting the global water-security challenge, he noted that billions of people worldwide continue to lack access to safe water and sanitation services. He emphasised that water security is fundamental to economic growth, employment generation, prosperity and social stability. He called for greater global investments in water and sanitation, stronger political commitment and enhanced partnerships, while also emphasising that Africa should be viewed not only through the lens of challenges but also as a source of innovation, enterprise and locally developed solutions. He welcomed the India-Africa dialogue and advocated for continued engagement and institutionalised cooperation between the two regions.
Representatives from the
World Bank
,
World Health Organization (WHO)
,
UNICEF
,
Sanitation and Water for All (SWA)
and
BISAG-N
shared international experiences, innovations and best practices in WASH service delivery. Discussions highlighted the increasing role of digital technologies, geospatial tools, community institutions, water-quality surveillance, climate resilience and evidence-based policymaking in strengthening water and sanitation systems. Participants also emphasised the importance of partnerships among governments, communities, development organisations and technology institutions for achieving sustainable WASH outcomes.
Mr. Yvan J.-F. Hutin, representing the World Health Organization (WHO), underscored the close links between safe drinking water, sanitation and public health outcomes, and highlighted the importance of water-quality surveillance, preventive health measures and resilient WASH systems. Mr. Paulos Workneh, Chief WASH, India, UNICEF, shared experiences on community-centred service delivery, behaviour change, inclusion and strengthening WASH services for women, children and vulnerable populations. Ms. Ruchika Shiva, Director, Global & Asia Regional Programme, Sanitation and Water for All (SWA), emphasised the importance of multi-stakeholder partnerships, country-led action, accountability and collaborative approaches for achieving universal access to water and sanitation. Dr. Vinay Thakur, Director General, BISAG-N, showcased the use of geospatial technologies, GIS-based planning and digital mapping solutions for monitoring water infrastructure, improving asset management and enabling data-driven decision-making in the WASH sector. Collectively, the speakers highlighted the growing role of digital innovation, climate resilience, community participation and evidence-based governance in strengthening sustainable WASH systems.
Addressing the gathering,
Shri Shivala Naik Mude, Additional Secretary, Ministry of External Affairs,
highlighted India's longstanding development partnership with African countries and reaffirmed the country's commitment to supporting Africa through infrastructure development, institutional capacity building and knowledge exchange. He noted that Digital Public Infrastructure, water-resource management and technical cooperation present significant opportunities for future India-Africa collaboration. Recalling the historical and civilisational ties between India and Africa, he emphasised the importance of working together as partners of the Global South to address common development challenges.
During the interactive session, Ambassadors and representatives of African countries shared experiences and perspectives on water security, sanitation, irrigation, climate resilience and sustainable infrastructure development in their countries. They acknowledged India's achievements in expanding access to drinking water and sanitation and highlighted several common priorities, including water harvesting, groundwater management, wastewater treatment and reuse, source sustainability, affordable water-treatment technologies, waste management, digital water governance and climate-resilient infrastructure.
The discussions underscored the need for practical, affordable and locally adaptable solutions, particularly for rural, drought-prone and underserved communities. African representatives also highlighted the importance of sustainable financing, effective operation and maintenance systems, institutional capacity building, private sector participation and development of local technical skills. Several participants expressed interest in pursuing government-to-government cooperation, technical exchanges, pilot projects, research partnerships, academic collaboration and exposure visits to facilitate knowledge sharing and technology transfer.
The day started with welcoming the participants by Shri D. Senthil Pandian, Joint Secretary, DDWS. He called the roundtable as an important platform for strengthening cooperation among countries facing similar development challenges. Focusing on the

opened new avenues for India-Africa cooperation in water security and sanitation

She highlighted knowledge exchange, capacity building, water-quality management, digital public infrastructure for WASH, community-led governance, climate-resilient water systems and sustainable sanitation as priority areas for future engagement. title: IIWW 2026: India and Netherlands Strengthen Strategic Partnership in Water Sector
subtitle: Two MoUs Signed for Technical Cooperation and Capacity Building on Kalpasar Project
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                24 SEP 2026 6:04PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Union Minister for Jal Shakti, Shri C. R. Patil and Vice Minister for Infrastructure and Water Management, Netherlands, H.E. Mr. Jaap Slootmaker, chaired a bilateral meeting between India and the Netherlands on the Strategic Partnership on Water at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, on the sidelines of the 9th India International Water Week (IIWW) 2026.
Minister of State for Jal Shakti Shri Raj Bhushan Choudhary, Minister of State for Water Resources and Water Supply (Independent Charge), Government of Gujarat, Shri Ishwarsinh Patel, Secretary, Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation Shri Ashok K.K. Meena, Secretary, Department of Water Resources, River Development and Ganga Rejuvenation Smt. Archana Varma, Chairman, Central Water Commission Shri Anupam Prasad, Ambassador of the Netherlands H.E. Ms. Marisa Gerards and other senior officials were also present.
The meeting provided an opportunity to review and further strengthen India–Netherlands cooperation in the water sector with particular focus on advancing technical cooperation for the Kalpasar Project in Gujarat. As part of the bilateral engagement, two Tripartite Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) were signed to facilitate cooperation for the Kalpasar Project between the Central Water Commission (CWC), Kalpasar Department, Government of Gujarat, and Dutch knowledge institutions Deltares and TU Delft.
Speaking on the occasion, Union Minister for Jal Shakti Shri C R Patil said that he was pleased to see Deltares and TU Delft entering into MoUs with their Indian counterparts to deepen cooperation in the execution of the Kalpasar Project and capacity building. He expressed confidence that the MoUs would provide a strong basis for both countries to work together towards the successful execution of the project.
The Minister noted that the Kalpasar Project was discussed during Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi’s visit to the Netherlands in May 2026, following which a Letter of Intent for technical cooperation was signed on 16 May 2026. He said that the project envisages creation of a freshwater reservoir using runoff from the Sabarmati, Mahi and Dhadhar rivers, supplemented by water conveyed from the Narmada River.
He further highlighted that during the Indian delegation’s visit to the Netherlands in July 2026, valuable insights were received in areas including flood protection, coastal infrastructure, hydraulic modelling, sluice and pumping systems, dyke technologies and ecological solutions. He noted that there were useful parallels with the Afsluitdijk in the Netherlands, particularly in terms of engineering, water management and coastal infrastructure.
Vice Minister for Infrastructure and Water Management of the Netherlands, H.E. Mr. Jaap Slootmaker, highlighted the importance of the Letter of Intent for technical cooperation on the Kalpasar Project and the opportunities it presents for further India–Netherlands cooperation. Referring to the Afsluitdijk, he said that the structure is nearly 100 years old and is now being renewed, providing an opportunity for the Netherlands to share the experience and knowledge accumulated over the past century. He added that Dutch institutions such as Deltares and TU Delft would contribute their expertise through the MoUs, providing a foundation for further collaboration in the water sector. He also emphasised the importance of sharing lessons learned, particularly in areas such as ecology and fish migration.
The MoUs will facilitate technical collaboration through sharing of Dutch expertise and advanced engineering practices for the planning, design and implementation of the project. The cooperation with Deltares, inter alia, covers technical review, hydraulic and hydrological modelling, coastal and structural engineering, climate resilience, capacity building, knowledge transfer and digital applications.

title: 4th Edition of Bharat CPSEs’ Consultative Conclave Inaugurated at Gati Shakti Vishwavidyalaya, Vadodara
subtitle:
Over 26 Senior Officers from 15 CPSEs of the Infrastructure, Transportation and Logistics Sectors, Subject Matter Experts from the academia and industry, Domain-Specific Faculty of GSV, Leading Industry Stalwarts, and Representatives of CBC and Union Ministries Converge on One Platform for Three-Day Consultative Deliberations on “Excellence in Project and Asset Management” under Mission Karmayogi

Conclave to Deliberate on PM Gati, ULIP, Multimodal Connectivity, Technology-Driven Asset Management and Global Best Practices, in Support of Viksit Bharat 2047
ministry: Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances & Pensions
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                24 SEP 2026 4:17PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The
Capacity Building Commission (CBC), Government of India, in collaboration with the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE),
Ministry of Finance, today inaugurated the
4th Edition of the Bharat CPSEs’ Consultative Conclave
at the Sabhagriha Auditorium, Gati Shakti Vishwavidyalaya (GSV), Vadodara. Convened under the Mission Karmayogi framework, with
GSV as the Strategic Knowledge Partner
, the three-day Conclave (24–26 September 2026) has brought together, on a single consultative platform, over
26 senior officers from 15 Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs)
of the Infrastructure & Construction and Transportation, Logistics & Telecommunication Services sectors, along with subject matter experts from the industry and academia, domain-specific faculty members of GSV, associated industry stalwarts, and senior representatives of CBC and Union Ministries.
The Conclave’s thematic focus on Transportation, Logistics and Infrastructure sector assumes particular significance against the backdrop of the Prime Minister’s “Sapta Dhara” vision - the Seven Streams of Strength for Viksit Bharat, in his Independence Day 2026 address, in which Gati Shakti, denoting the creation of sustainable, world-class quality infrastructure, was identified as the fourth stream driving India’s development journey.
Inaugural Session
The Inaugural Session opened with a ceremonial lighting of the lamp by the dignitaries.
Prof. Kaushik Das, Program Director from GSV
and the CBC Task Force Member
, presented an overview of the outcomes of Batch I of the Conclave and outlined the theme and objectives of the 4th Edition, followed by an inaugural address by
Dr Alka Mittal, Member (Administration), CBC
, and the context setting address by
Prof. (Dr.) Manoj Choudhary, Hon’ble Vice Chancellor, GSV
. This was followed by the Keynote Address of the Chief Guest of the event,
Shri Anil Kumar Lahoti, Chairman, Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI)
. The inaugural session concluded with a presentation on the findings of the pre-event diagnostic survey by
Shri Sumeet Singh, Director, CBC
.
Dr. Nalin Shinghal, former CMD of BHEL and CEL,
was welcomed by the Vice-Chancellor as the Program Mentor for the event.
A First-of-its-Kind Consultative Platform for Evidence-Based Governance
The Bharat CPSEs’ Consultative Conclave, conceptualised by CBC and supported by the Strategic Knowledge Partnership of GSV, given its extensive domain leadership in transportation, logistics and infrastructure, is the first initiative of its kind in India. By bringing public and private industry players, academic faculty and government officers together on one platform, the Conclave embodies a genuinely consultative model of capacity building, which is structured and designed keeping in view the practical challenges of project and asset management, as assessed directly from industry demand.
The knowledge briefs and documents emerging from the Conclave — culminating in the Bharat CPSE Compendium and an addressee-specific Reform Agenda — together with the extensive cross-learning generated among CPSEs, ministries, industry and academia, are expected to lend this institutionalised platform the stature of a thought-leadership - one that can guide and inform evidence-based decision-making, policy formulation and policy reform in India’s project and asset management ecosystem, in line with the vision articulated by the Hon’ble Prime Minister.
Three Days of Interactive, Participatory Capacity Building
Over the next two days, the Conclave moves into a series of thematic and breakout sessions structured entirely around industry-identified challenges in project and asset management — conceived as an interactive and participatory capacity-building exercise rather than a conventional lecture format.
The programme will conclude with an experiential learning field visit to the GSV Airbus Centre of Excellence, the Sardar Sarovar Dam and Statue of Unity at Kevadia, offering participants a first-hand view of large-scale infrastructure and project management in action.
“Kshamta SANGAM” Pre-Launch Joint Declaration: A New National Platform for Academia–Government-Industry Partnership all set for national launch in coming weeks
In a significant development during the Inaugural Session, CBC and GSV jointly declared to collaborate on its upcoming initiative -
Kshamta SANGAM — Strategizing Atmanirbhar National Governance through Academia Mobilization
. It will strategically leverage the collective knowledge resources and innovations of academia for futuristic capacity building and evidence-based governance in a systematic, scientific and outcome-oriented manner.
Gati Shakti Vishwavidyalaya today became the first academic institution to come on board this national mission, with the pre-launch Joint Declaration made by CBC and GSV, committing to take the initiative forward towards its official national launch in coming weeks under Mission Karmayogi.

content:
Indian Railways has approved the construction of a four-lane Road Over Bridge (ROB) at Alkapuri in Vadodara Division of Western Railway at a total cost of ₹166.5 crore, on a cost-sharing basis with the State Government.
The total project cost will be shared equally between Indian Railways and the State Government. The Railway share will be approximately ₹83.2769 crore, while the State Government share will also be approximately ₹83.2769 crore.
Four-Lane ROB to Augment Existing Road Connectivity
The existing Alkapuri Road Under Bridge (RUB) near Vadodara Railway Station serves as an important east-west road connectivity link between the Alkapuri and Kalaghoda areas of Vadodara city. However, the existing RUB has a vertical clearance of only about 3.0 metres, resulting in restrictions on the movement of larger vehicles and recurring waterlogging during the monsoon.
These limitations contribute to traffic congestion, operational difficulties and inconvenience for road users. The four-lane grade-separated road facility will augment the capacity and functionality of the existing road crossing arrangement.
Improved Connectivity to Key Transport Facilities
The ROB will provide an improved and more effective crossing facility without disturbing railway operations. It will also provide important connectivity to Vadodara Railway Station, GSRTC Bus Station and the upcoming High-Speed Rail (Bullet Train) Station.
Addressing Growing Traffic Requirements
The traffic assessment indicates peak-hour traffic of more than 1,600 PCU per hour, along with multiple traffic conflict points and inadequate pedestrian facilities. The existing RUB has consequently become inadequate to cater to the present and projected traffic requirements of the area.
The four-lane grade-separated facility will address the functional limitations of the existing RUB while augmenting road connectivity in this important part of Vadodara.
The project will strengthen the connectivity around Vadodara Railway Station while providing a more effective crossing arrangement and addressing the limitations of the existing Alkapuri RUB.

title: NHAI Guidelines to Strengthen Technology Integration and Sustainability in Development of High-Speed National Highway Corridors
subtitle: New guidelines focus on better planning, modern technology, smoother tolling, improved drainage and greener corridors
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                24 SEP 2026 4:27PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Taking significant step towards developing a world-class National Highway network, National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) has released comprehensive guidelines for the planning and design of High-Speed Access-Controlled National Highways, other than Expressways. The new guidelines are aimed at ensuring that the High- speed National Highways are better designed & planned, safer, greener and ready to meet the needs of future traffic. The guidelines will apply to all upcoming four and six-lane Greenfield and Brownfield High-Speed Access-Controlled National Highways.
Data-Driven Planning for Future Traffic
The guidelines lay emphasis on comprehensive traffic assessment and future demand planning. Traffic projections shall take into account existing and diverted traffic, along with expected growth in freight movement linked to economic and commercial activities. Toll data and other reliable sources will also be used to make traffic estimates more accurate.
Technology-Enabled Construction
Use of modern technology will be enhanced during the construction of High-speed National Highways to improve quality, accuracy and monitoring. The guidelines provide for the use of Automated and Intelligent Machine-aided Construction (AI-MC) technology for construction of embankments and highway pavements, in accordance with applicable Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH) guidelines. Incorporation of these measures will facilitate technology-enabled construction, enabling better quality, consistency and monitoring during National Highway development. Also as envisioned by the Government of India, a shift will be made to install Multi Lane Free Flow (MLFF) system of tolling on High-speed corridors, provisions for implementation of MLFF shall be made accordingly.
Landscaping and Environmental Measures from Planning Stage
Landscaping and plantation will be incorporated as an integral part of project planning. Landscaping and plantations will be planned at suitable locations such as loop areas, below flyovers, medians and other suitable locations, keeping in view local climate, topography and environmental conditions. Drip irrigation systems will also be provided on National Highway medians, to ensure efficient use of water and easier maintenance of plantations.
Better Drainage and Water Management
Comprehensive drainage planning will form an integral part of the DPR process. The planning will identify where rainwater will be disposed and how water from the National Highway and surrounding areas will be safely managed. Water harvesting structures will also be provided in loop areas and other suitable locations, particularly with no natural outlet for rainwater.
Special arrangements will be made to manage water around underpasses flyovers depressed medians and other structures, helping to prevent water logging and damage to the National Highway infrastructure. Drainage plans will clearly identify water disposal points and provide suitable arrangements for managing rainwater from the high-speed National Highways and surrounding areas.
The guidelines will significantly contribute towards development of safer, more sustainable and future-ready High Speed National Highway corridors across the country.

content:
Union Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Science & Technology, Earth Sciences and MoS PMO, Personnel, Public Grievances, Pensions, Atomic Energy and Space, Dr. Jitendra Singh today formally launched the commercial use of bio-based biodegradable plastic based on Polylactic Acid (PLA), marking an important step in India’s transition towards next-generation sustainable manufacturing.
The initiative, being taken forward by Balrampur Chini Mills Limited (BCML) under the Government’s BioE3 (Biotechnology for Economy, Environment & Employment) framework, combines biotechnology, sustainable manufacturing and commercial translation. A ₹75 crore grant from the Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council (BIRAC), under the Department of Biotechnology (DBT), is supporting the 100 TPA pilot-scale R&D facility for PLA and co-polymers, aimed at developing advanced bio-based materials and facilitating their translation towards commercial production.
The initiative was unveiled at the Department of Biotechnology, Ministry of Science & Technology, in New Delhi. The pilot-scale facility will be established at BCML’s integrated manufacturing complex at Kumbhi, Uttar Pradesh, where it will support the development and scale-up of PLA and co-polymer technologies for sustainable material applications.
Speaking on the occasion, Dr. Jitendra Singh said the initiative represents a significant milestone in India’s bioeconomy journey, where biotechnology is moving beyond laboratory research towards commercial products, sustainable manufacturing and employment generation. He said India’s bioeconomy, which was around US$10 billion in 2014, has grown to nearly
US$195 billion, reflecting the rapid expansion of biotechnology-led economic activity. He said the next phase must focus on translating scientific capabilities into commercially viable products and technologies.
Dr. Jitendra Singh said the PLA initiative can strengthen India’s ability to participate in the global transition towards sustainable manufacturing and create a new value chain based on biological resources. He said the project demonstrates how indigenous scientific capabilities can be connected with industrial production to create high-value materials while addressing environmental concerns. The initiative, he added, can contribute to India’s emergence as a global leader in the bioeconomy and as a source of practical solutions for other countries.
A major focus of the Minister’s address was the “waste to wealth” approach. Dr. Jitendra Singh said India’s diversity means that different regions generate different kinds of biomass and waste, requiring different technologies and methodologies for conversion into useful products. Region-specific biotechnology capabilities, he said, can therefore help convert locally available resources into wealth while creating new opportunities for regional development.
“There is no such thing as waste,” Dr. Jitendra Singh said, stressing that materials described as waste often contain significant underlying value that can be unlocked through science and technology. He said India’s diverse experience with biological resources, recycling and biomass conversion gives the country an opportunity to develop solutions that can have wider global relevance.
The Minister said the commercial translation of research must happen at an early stage, with technologies moving from laboratories to markets through pilot facilities, validation, skilled manpower and industry participation. He said the PLA facility can become a platform for developing polymers for high-value applications, training skilled personnel and generating the knowledge and experience required for commercial-scale manufacturing.
The 100 TPA pilot-scale R&D facility will focus on developing specialised PLA grades and advanced PLA co-polymers for high-value applications. It will generate techno-economic data and process know-how, support product development and customer validation, facilitate technology indigenisation and help enable seamless scale-up towards commercial production. The facility will also strengthen collaboration between industry, academia and research institutions.
Dr. Jitendra Singh also called for greater public outreach to explain biotechnology in simple and relatable terms. He suggested that communication around such technologies should show how everyday agricultural resources such as sugarcane can be converted into products beyond food, including sustainable materials. He said such storytelling can help people understand the value of biotechnology, encourage wider adoption and support the commercial use of indigenous technologies.
Linking the initiative with the Government’s “Vocal for Local and Global” approach, Dr. Jitendra Singh said India should build indigenous commercial production capabilities and take successful technologies from local development to global markets. He said the BioE3 framework provides an opportunity to simultaneously advance the country’s economic growth, environmental sustainability and employment objectives.
The PLA initiative also marks a significant diversification of India’s bio-based manufacturing landscape. BCML’s commercial PLA venture is based on converting renewable sugar-based feedstock into PLA and bioplastics, creating a pathway from agricultural resources to sustainable materials. The company has projected its commercial PLA facility as an industrial-scale bio-plastic venture, while the BioE3-supported pilot facility will provide an innovation and R&D platform for next-generation PLA grades and co-polymers.
Speaking on the occasion, Dr. Rajesh Sudhir Gokhale, Secretary, DBT, DG-BRIC and Chairman, BIRAC, said the initiative takes biotechnology beyond laboratory science towards an integrated manufacturing ecosystem involving validated processes, pilot facilities, skilling and commercial-scale production. He said the project can create a new value chain beyond ethanol by converting biological resources such as sugar and other biomass into lactic acid and high-value biopolymers, while creating opportunities for sustainable development, employment and regional growth.
Present on the occasion were Secretary, DBT, Director General, BRIC and Chairman, BIRAC, Dr. Rajesh Sudhir Gokhale; Dr. Dhananjay K. Tiwary, Scientist-H, DBT and Managing Director, BIRAC; Ms. Ekta Vishnoi, Joint Secretary, DBT; Dr. Kalaivani Ganesan, DBT; Dr. Shilpi Gupta, BIRAC; and Ms. Avantika Saraogi, Executive Director, Balrampur Chini Mills Limited, among others.
The BioE3-backed initiative is expected to accelerate the development and commercialisation of advanced bio-based materials, strengthen India’s indigenous biomanufacturing capabilities and support the emergence of a sustainable, employment-generating and globally competitive bioeconomy.

title: TDB-DST signs agreement with GalaxEye for ₹63.84 crore RDI support to develop next-generation multisensor satellite technology
subtitle: Indigenous OptoSAR technology to combine SAR and optical imaging for high-resolution Earth observation
date:

content:
Taking forward the Government of India’s push to accelerate private-sector research and development in strategic and emerging technologies, the Technology Development Board (TDB), Department of Science & Technology (DST), Government of India, has signed an agreement with M/s GalaxEye Space Solutions Private Limited, Bengaluru for financial support of ₹63.84 crore under the Research Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund.
The project, with a total approved cost of ₹247.69 crore, is aimed at developing a multisensor satellite capable of high-resolution (<0.5 m) OptoSAR imaging and taking the technology from TRL-6 to TRL-9. The support will be extended through Optionally Convertible Debentures (OCD). At the heart of the GalaxEye project is OptoSAR, an approach that brings together two fundamentally different ways of observing the Earth — Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) and Electro-Optical (EO) imaging.
While optical imaging can provide highly detailed visual information, its effectiveness can be affected by cloud cover and illumination. SAR, on the other hand, can operate irrespective of daylight and can image through cloud cover. The proposed system seeks to bring these complementary capabilities together through fusion of SAR and EO data, enabling a richer and more continuous picture of the Earth.
The proposed satellite is designed to provide sub-0.5 metre high-resolution imaging. The technology is intended to support applications including wide-area and long-range surveillance, human and vehicle detection, and target classification, while enabling imaging across diverse weather and lighting conditions.
The project represents a significant technology-maturation programme, with the RDI support enabling GalaxEye to undertake further development, engineering, testing and validation required to progress the technology from TRL-6 to TRL-9.
Sh. Rajesh Kumar Pathak, Secretary, TDB,
said,
“India’s space ecosystem is entering a phase where the ability to develop and deploy sophisticated technologies within the country will be increasingly important. The RDI Fund provides an important mechanism to support such technology-intensive efforts through the critical stages between advanced development and deployment. The agreement with GalaxEye reflects TDB’s focus on enabling indigenous capabilities in emerging space technologies and supporting their journey towards commercialisation.”
Promoters of GalaxEye Space Solutions Private Limited said
,“The support from the Technology Development Board under the RDI Fund will enable us to accelerate the development and validation of our OptoSAR technology. By combining SAR and optical sensing, we are working towards an Earth-observation capability that can provide high-resolution information across a wider range of weather and lighting conditions. This partnership will be important in taking the technology towards TRL-9 and its subsequent deployment.”

title: Beyond one: Indian researchers’ experiment could lead to a new tool for quantum measurement
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                24 SEP 2026 3:07PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Researchers have made the first experimental measurement of a quantum measure exceeding one, beyond the upper limit of ordinary probability. The result brings Quantum Measure Theory (QMT), a framework rooted in quantum foundations and the search for quantum gravity, into the laboratory, with potential applications in quantum measurement and computing.
Quantum mechanics is usually described in terms of the state of a system at a particular time and the outcomes obtained when we measure it. A complementary viewpoint is to describe a quantum system through its possible histories, meaning the different ways it can evolve between preparation and detection or the path that the photon could take in an experiment from a laser to a detector. QMT assigns a generalized measure to sets of such histories, incorporating the interference between them. Unlike an ordinary probability, this quantum measure can exceed one.
The difficulty is that a general set of histories does not necessarily correspond to a sequence of ordinary measurements, so its quantum measure is not straightforward to access experimentally.
An experiment by the Raman Research Institute (RRI), an autonomous institute of the Department of Science and Technology (DST) has now measured the quantum measure assigned to a chosen collection of possible photon paths between the laser source and the detector.
In a future implementation, a filter could select a chosen collection of photon paths while leaving the photons available for further quantum operations. That could potentially turn this “event-filtering” into a new tool for quantum measurement and quantum computing.
To make QMT experimentally accessible, RRI physicists started constructing an “event-filter” that would select a set of photon routes (called event). Sanchari Chakraborti, then a PhD student at RRI, performed the experiment under the supervision of Urbasi Sinha, the paper’s co-author and senior professor at RRI.
To build this event-filter, they allowed the photons in the laser beam to traverse different routes in their optical setup. They then used polarisation, which tells the orientation in which the light waves are oscillating, to distinguish different routes and select the particular collection of routes they wanted. Later, they erased the distinguishing information so that the routes could interfere. In the reported experiment, published in the journal Quantum, the researchers measured input and output laser powers to infer the photon-detection probability. They then used the event-filter’s calibration to determine the “quantum measure”.
The quantum measure assigns a weight to a chosen collection of photon routes. They measured a quantum measure of about 1.17, agreeing within experimental uncertainty with the prediction of about 1.18 after accounting for imperfections in the apparatus. The value 1.17 showed that the quantum measure was behaving differently from ordinary classical probability that cannot exceed one.
Then how did the quantum measure exceed one? In the quantum world, contributions from different possible photon routes can also interfere with one another like waves: when two waves’ crests overlap, they create a bigger wave. This allows the quantum measure that includes interference between the routes to exceed one. The important caveat is that they didn’t measure a probability greater than one. The detector probability remains an ordinary probability below one. What can exceed one is the quantum measure.
Fig.: Event-filtering of quantum histories.
An optical field explores multiple possible histories. The event filter selects a chosen set of histories while preserving the interference needed to determine their quantum measure. The measured result, μ(E)
≅
1.17, exceeds the classical probability bound of unity, even though the inferred photon-detection probability itself remains between zero and one. (Credit: Urbasi Sinha, RRI)
The study demonstrates for the first time the measurement of a quantum measure exceeding one. It shows that this quantity is not merely an abstract concept that can be calculated on paper: it can be measured experimentally. “There is something particularly satisfying about seeing an idea that grew out of fundamental questions about quantum mechanics become an optical experiment on a laboratory table. We’re not claiming that this resolves the quantum measurement problem,” says Sinha. “But we’ve enlarged the class of questions about quantum processes that can be connected to an experimental measurement.”
The quantum measure is central to QMT, which co-author
Rafael Sorkin
developed partly in the search for quantum gravity. Its focus on complete histories makes it a natural framework for describing quantum processes across spacetime. This experiment brings that framework into the laboratory; it does not test a theory of quantum gravity.
Sorkin, a
researcher emeritus at Canada’s Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics
and a Distinguished Visiting Faculty member at RRI, passed away on 12 September 2026, shortly after the paper was accepted.
“This paper means a great deal to me personally as well as scientifically,” says Sinha.
Publication Link:
https://doi.org/10.22331/q-2026-09-24-2215

title: NCSC Chairman Shri Kishor Makwana Conducts Spot Inquiry at IIT Bombay in Connection with Death of Scheduled Caste Student

date:

content:
The Hon’ble Chairman of the National Commission for Scheduled Castes (NCSC), Shri Kishor Makwana, today conducted a detailed spot inquiry at the Indian Institute of Technology Bombay (IIT Bombay) in connection with the death of Shri Sahil Wakode, a Scheduled Caste student pursuing his second year of B.Tech. in the Department of Energy Science and Engineering.
The visit was undertaken in view of the allegations levelled by the family of the deceased regarding caste-based discrimination, harassment and the circumstances preceding his death. The matter is presently under investigation by the Mumbai Police Crime Branch. The Commission is examining the matter within the framework of the constitutional and statutory safeguards available to members of the Scheduled Castes.
During the visit, the Hon’ble Chairman held a detailed interaction with senior authorities of IIT Bombay, including the Director, Deputy Director, Registrar, concerned faculty members and other officials of the Institute. The Commission sought a comprehensive account of the sequence of events preceding the student’s death, including the incident reported to have occurred during a mid-semester examination on 18 September 2026, when the student was allegedly found involved in academic malpractice.
The Commission examined the circumstances in which the student was questioned during the examination, the procedure reportedly followed thereafter, the role of the concerned faculty and Institute authorities, and the institutional mechanisms available for addressing student grievances and safeguarding the welfare and rights of students belonging to Scheduled Castes.
The Hon’ble Chairman emphasized that all relevant records and material connected with the matter, including CCTV footage, electronic evidence, official communications, examination-related records and other documentary material, should be preserved and made available to the investigating authorities in accordance with law, so that the circumstances surrounding the student’s death can be established on the basis of evidence.
As part of the spot inquiry, Shri Kishor Makwana personally visited the Department of Energy Science and Engineering, where Shri Sahil Wakode was pursuing his studies. The Chairman also inspected the classroom/examination hall where the reported examination incident took place and sought information regarding the sequence of events during and immediately after the examination.
The Commission thereafter visited the hostel premises and the room occupied by the deceased student. The Hon’ble Chairman also interacted with classmates and fellow students of Shri Sahil Wakode to understand his academic and campus experience and to obtain information regarding the circumstances and events preceding his death. The Commission is seeking to consider such inputs along with official records and the findings of the ongoing investigation.
Following the spot inquiry at IIT Bombay, the Hon’ble Chairman held a high-level meeting with senior police authorities, including the Director General of Police, Commissioner of Police and senior officers associated with the investigation, including officers of the Crime Branch.
During the meeting, the Commission reviewed the status and progress of the investigation and sought details regarding the FIR, collection and preservation of evidence, CCTV footage, examination of witnesses and other relevant aspects of the case.
The Hon’ble Chairman directed the investigating authorities to ensure that the investigation is fair, impartial, comprehensive and expeditious, and that every relevant allegation and circumstance is examined strictly on the basis of available evidence and in accordance with law.
The police authorities were further asked to ensure proper collection, preservation and examination of all relevant documentary, electronic, forensic and testimonial evidence. The Commission also emphasized the need for recording the statements of students, faculty members, Institute officials and other persons who may possess relevant information, wherever required in accordance with law.
The Hon’ble Chairman directed the concerned authorities to furnish a detailed Action Taken/Investigation Report to the National Commission for Scheduled Castes at the earliest, for further examination by the Commission.
The Hon’ble Chairman subsequently met the parents and other family members of Shri Sahil Wakode and heard their grievances and concerns in detail. The family placed before the Commission their allegations regarding the circumstances preceding the death of the student and submitted a written complaint seeking appropriate intervention by the Commission.
Shri Makwana assured the family that the Commission would examine the matter in accordance with its constitutional and statutory mandate. The Commission will closely monitor the progress of the investigation and take appropriate action within its jurisdiction based on the facts and evidence that emerge.
The Commission reiterated that the constitutional and statutory safeguards available to members of the Scheduled Castes must be effectively protected and that institutions must maintain appropriate mechanisms for ensuring dignity, equality, non-discrimination, student welfare and effective grievance redressal.
The Commission also emphasized the importance of maintaining social harmony and cohesion while ensuring that all allegations are examined objectively, transparently and in accordance with due process.
The Hon’ble Chairman was accompanied by Dr. Sunil Kumar Babu, Director, NCSC State Office, Maharashtra; Dr. R. Stalin, Deputy Director, Atrocities & Protection of Civil Rights (APCR) Wing, NCSC Headquarters, New Delhi; and officials of the NCSC State Office.

A Senior Official in the Corporation informed that members of notified Other Backward Classes with an annual family income of up to ₹5 lakh may seek assistance for activities with the potential to generate sustainable income, subject to the applicable eligibility requirements and the channel partner’s processes.
He said under the Individual Loan Scheme, assistance can cover up to 85% of project cost, with a maximum loan of ₹25 lakh per beneficiary. Loans of up to ₹1.25 lakh carry a beneficiary interest rate of 7% per annum, while loans above ₹1.25 lakh and up to ₹25 lakh carry a rate of 8% per annum, he added.
The NBCFDC Official said that education loans of up to ₹25 lakh are available at a beneficiary interest rate of 8% per annum, with a repayment period of up to 10 years inclusive of the moratorium period, as per the conditions prescribed by NBCFDC.
He said the Corporation promotes economic and developmental activities, skill development and self-employment, which was incorporated on January 13, 1992,
The NBCFDC Official further said that the Group Loan Scheme provides assistance to self-help groups of up to ₹25 lakh per group, subject to a limit of ₹1.25 lakh per beneficiary adding that loans through State Channelizing Agencies or banks can cover up to 90% of project cost at a beneficiary interest rate of 7% per annum. He added that at least 60% of the group’s members must belong to Backward Classes; the other members may belong to eligible weaker sections.
It is pertinent to mention that NBCFDC’s published pattern of finance provides for an annual timely payment rebate of 1%, shared equally between the channel partner and beneficiary. Eligible applicants can approach the relevant channel partner in their district or submit a request through the registration portal on the NBCFDC website.
For scheme details and applications, the interested applicants may visit

2nd to 31st October 2026

e-waste

while institutionalizing Swachhata across the Department and its organizations.

Department of Administrative Reforms & Public Grievances (DARPG)

Preparatory Phase from 16th to 30th September 2026

Implementation Phase from 2nd to 31st October 2026

Swachhata and good governance

The campaign will seek to convert idle records, redundant material and pending matters into opportunities for greater efficiency, accountability and productivity.
DEPwD is committed to making Special Campaign 6.0 a meaningful and outcome-oriented exercise. Concerted efforts will be undertaken by the Department and its organizations to achieve the targets identified during the preparatory phase and to carry forward the culture of cleanliness, timely disposal and efficient use of public resources as an integral part of everyday governance.

Steel Authority of India Limited (SAIL) held its 54th Annual General Meeting (AGM) today on 24.09.2026, in hybrid mode at CSOI, New Delhi. Addressing the shareholders, Chairman & Managing Director Dr. A.K. Panda presented the Company’s performance for FY 2025–26 and outlined its strategic priorities for the years ahead.
SAIL CMD, Dr. Panda noted that despite a challenging global steel environment marked by geopolitical uncertainties and market volatility, India continued to lead global steel demand growth, retaining its position as the world’s fastest growing major steel producer. He stated that, “SAIL demonstrated strong resilience and adaptability, achieving new benchmarks driven by technological upgrades, financial prudence, digitalisation, HR initiatives and sustainability efforts.”
Dr. Panda emphasised that, “SAIL’s performance during the year was marked not only by best-ever crude steel, finished steel and saleable steel production, but also a strong focus towards value creation
.
The Company produced 10.7 Million Tonnes (MT) of value-added steel
,
which was 56% of total saleable steel, up by 7% over FY'24-25, and introduced 28 new products across infrastructure, automotive, energy and manufacturing sectors - significantly strengthening SAIL’s ability to meet evolving national and sectoral requirements. He added that this enhanced product capability directly reinforced SAIL’s nation-building role. In FY 2025–26, the Company dispatched the first consignment of indigenously developed Vande Bharat wheels
and supplied steel for five Indian Navy ships - INS Arnala, Udaygiri, Himgiri, Androth and Anjadeep - commissioned during the year. Dr. Panda reiterated SAIL’s commitment to contributing to Viksit Bharat 2047
,
aligned with the National Steel Policy.
Highlighting the Company’s financial performance, Dr. Panda said, “Reflecting operational efficiency, in FY 2025–26 SAIL posted its highest ever revenue, surpassing ₹1,09,000 crore, an 8% increase over the previous year. Borrowings were reduced by more than ₹5,000 crore through judicious fund management. With higher sales volume, lower inventory and reduced borrowings, the Company’s profitability strengthened, and both PBT & PAT improved by 44% and 50.5% respectively. The Board has recommended a Final Dividend of ₹2.35 per equity share.”
Reinforcing the Company’s sustainability focus, CMD shared that SAIL generated 5.61 million units of green power from the first 4 MW floating solar plant at IISCO Steel Plant, with a 20 MW floating solar plant underway at Bhilai Steel Plant. Additionally, 278.5 MW of solar projects are under consideration across various plants. Looking ahead, Dr Panda stated that, “SAIL is focused on expanding crude steel capacity to ~35 MTPA by FY 2030–31, supported by green capacity creation, adoption of low-carbon technologies, digital enablement, enhanced customer engagement, increased share of value-added and special steels, and deeper integration with retail and MSME ecosystems.”

title: Review of Constitutional Safeguards and Implementation of Development Schemes for Scheduled Tribes in the State of Karnataka
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                24 SEP 2026 5:08PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (NCST) today undertook a comprehensive review of the implementation of constitutional safeguards, welfare measures and development programmes for Scheduled Tribes in Karnataka at a review meeting held at the Conference Hall of Radisson Blu, Bengaluru.
The review meeting was chaired by Shri Antar Singh Arya, Hon’ble Chairperson, NCST, and was attended by Shri Jatothu Hussain, Hon'ble Member and Shri Amit Nirmal, Joint Secretary, NCST, and senior officers of the Commission.
The State Government was represented by the Chief Secretary, Director General of Police, Additional Chief Secretaries, Principal Secretaries and Secretaries of various departments, along with other senior officers. The review was undertaken on the basis of a structured and detailed questionnaire circulated by the Commission in advance, the information and data furnished by the Government of Karnataka, grievances and petitions received from members of the Scheduled Tribe communities, feedback received prior to the review meeting, and observations arising from field visits previously undertaken by the Commission in the State of Karnataka.
During the review, the Commission examined a wide range of issues concerning the Scheduled Tribes of the State, including implementation of constitutional safeguards, reservation and backlog vacancies, utilisation of funds under the ST Component, tribal land and forest rights, implementation of the Forest Rights Act, educational and welfare measures, and institutional mechanisms for protection of tribal interests.
The Commission particularly reviewed concerns relating to the rejection of a substantial number of claims under the Forest Rights Act, 2006, and emphasised the need for a comprehensive examination of rejected and pending claims in accordance with the provisions of the Act and Rules.
The Commission also discussed the proposal for establishment of an exclusive Karnataka State Commission for Scheduled Tribes for continuous monitoring of constitutional safeguards, along with measures for filling backlog vacancies and ensuring effective representation of Scheduled Tribes in education and public employment.
Special emphasis was placed on the socio-economic and infrastructure development of Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs), particularly the Koraga and Jenu Kuruba communities, with focus on health, nutrition, housing, education, livelihoods, land and forest rights and access to basic services.
The meeting provided an important platform for detailed interaction between the Commission and the State Government on the status of implementation of various safeguards and development measures. The discussions were constructive and fruitful, and the Commission urged the concerned departments to take appropriate and time-bound action on the issues raised during the review.
The NCST reiterated its commitment to ensuring that constitutional safeguards and welfare measures intended for the Scheduled Tribes translate into tangible and equitable outcomes on the ground.
